items.name: Herders, Farmers & Iron Age
items.description: Kenya's Rift Valley and Lake Turkana basin hold some of the richest early-human fossil records on Earth, including the 'Turkana Boy' skeleton of Homo erectus, roughly 1.5 million years old. Within the span shown here, herding peoples spread through the region from around 3000 BCE (the Pastoral Neolithic), and Bantu-speaking farmers bringing iron working arrived during the first millennium CE, laying the foundations of Kenya's later Bantu, Nilotic, and Cushitic communities. Dates are approximate.

items.name: Swahili City-States
items.description: Along the coast, towns such as Mombasa, Malindi, Lamu, and Gedi grew into Swahili city-states that traded ivory, gold, and other goods across the Indian Ocean with Arabia, Persia, India, and China. Swahili, a Bantu language with many Arabic loanwords, became the coast's lingua franca, and Islam spread through its merchant elites. Ships of the Ming admiral Zheng He's fleets reached Malindi in the early 15th century.

items.name: Portuguese & Omani Coast
items.description: Vasco da Gama called at Malindi in 1498, and the Portuguese came to dominate the coast, building Fort Jesus in Mombasa in 1593. The Omani Arabs captured Fort Jesus in 1698 after a long siege, and the coast later fell under the Sultanate of Zanzibar, whose plantation economy relied on enslaved labour from the interior.

items.name: British East Africa
items.description: Britain declared the East Africa Protectorate in 1895 and built the Uganda Railway from Mombasa to Lake Victoria (1896–1901); Nairobi began as a railway depot in 1899. The fertile 'White Highlands' were reserved for European settlers, and African land loss and forced labour fuelled resentment. The territory became Kenya Colony in 1920, and early political organisers such as Harry Thuku were arrested.

items.name: Mau Mau Uprising & Emergency
items.description: The Mau Mau rebellion, rooted mainly among the Kikuyu over land and freedom, led Britain to declare a state of emergency in October 1952. Jomo Kenyatta was jailed after the Kapenguria trial, and the colonial government detained tens of thousands of people in camps where torture and abuse were widespread. The rebel leader Dedan Kimathi was captured in 1956 and executed in 1957. In 2013 the British government expressed regret and agreed a settlement with more than 5,000 Kenyan victims.

sources.title: GOV.UK — Statement to Parliament on settlement of Mau Mau claims (2013)

items.name: Independence: Kenyatta & Moi
items.description: Kenya became independent on 12 December 1963 and a republic a year later, with Jomo Kenyatta as president. Daniel arap Moi succeeded him in 1978 and made Kenya a one-party state by law in 1982. Domestic and international pressure restored multiparty politics in 1991, but Moi's KANU party kept power until 2002. The 1998 bombing of the US embassy in Nairobi killed more than 200 people.

items.name: Modern Kenya
items.description: Mwai Kibaki's 2002 victory ended KANU's long rule. The disputed 2007 election triggered violence that killed more than 1,000 people, leading to a power-sharing deal and a new constitution in 2010 that devolved power to counties. Kenya also became a pioneer of mobile money with M-Pesa, launched in 2007. Wangari Maathai, founder of the Green Belt Movement, became the first African woman to win the Nobel Peace Prize in 2004.
